standard.title: Fundamental movement in varied situations
standard.description: practise fundamental movement skills and apply them in a variety of movement situations
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have practised fundamental movement skills in minor game and play situations (AC9HPFM01). They have experimented with different ways of moving their body safely and manipulating objects and space (AC9HPFM02).
standard.progression_endpoint: Students practise fundamental movement skills and apply them in a variety of movement situations.

nodes.label: Locomotor and non-locomotor movement
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can perform locomotor movements using different body parts to travel in different directions, and perform non-locomotor balances.
nodes.minimum_width: Perform at least two locomotor movements (e.g. run, jump) in two directions; hold a balance and describe what helps maintain a stable position.
nodes.typical_width: Demonstrate a range of locomotor movements using different body parts across multiple directions and levels; perform and describe balances including what contributes to stability.
wider: Practise gliding forward and backward in the water using arm and kicking movements, comparing water movement to land-based locomotion
Sequence locomotor movements into a short movement phrase, varying direction, speed and level
Explore First Nations Australian movement games that use specific locomotor patterns
nodes.hinge_reason: Locomotor and balance competence underpins all subsequent application tasks. Students who cannot reliably execute a core movement pattern in isolation will not be able to select and implement skills in game situations (Node 2) or control objects while moving (Node 3).

response_modes.reason: Fluency in basic locomotor patterns and balance needs repetition across varied settings before application becomes possible. Focus practice on one or two movement forms across multiple activities rather than sampling many forms once.
Vary the surfaces, spaces and directions used so students experience the movement in different physical environments, reducing reliance on a single learned setting.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Locomotor movement in water, at different levels, and in structured sequences offers rich cross-context transfer. Students who can apply the same locomotor skill across qualitatively different environments (land, water, rhythm-based) build broader and more flexible movement foundations.
success_criteria: Performs at least two locomotor movements using different body parts in at least two directions
Holds a balance and can name one thing that helps them stay stable

nodes.label: Selecting and applying movement skills in games
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can select and implement different movement skills to be successful in a range of games.
nodes.minimum_width: In at least one minor game, select an appropriate movement skill and use it purposefully to participate successfully.
nodes.typical_width: Across a range of minor games, select and implement movement skills appropriate to the game context; describe why they chose a particular movement.
wider: Invent a new game using known movement skills and reflect on whether the movement choices made the game interesting and challenging
Participate in children's games from First Nations Australian cultures and identify which movement skills are used
Modify a familiar game to require a different movement skill and evaluate whether the change improves the game
nodes.hinge_reason: The ability to select movement skills purposefully — not just perform them in isolation — is the core transfer move of this descriptor. Thin treatment here leaves students able to perform skills in drills but unable to apply them in context, which undermines all subsequent movement application across the band.

response_modes.reason: Make the selection process explicit: before and after games, ask students why they chose a particular movement. Brief verbal or visual prompts help students articulate skill choice rather than just performing habitually.
Vary game types (chasing, fielding, net, target) so students practise selection across different movement demands rather than optimising for one game context.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Game variety offers genuine breadth — different game structures require different movement skill profiles, and students who have selected and applied skills across multiple game types develop more transferable movement decision-making.
success_criteria: In a game situation, selects a movement skill appropriate to what the game requires
Can describe why they used a particular movement in at least one game

nodes.label: Controlling objects with equipment and body parts
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can perform fundamental movement skills involving controlling objects with equipment and different parts of the body.
nodes.minimum_width: Use at least one piece of equipment to control a moving object; attempt control using a non-dominant body part.
nodes.typical_width: Use a range of equipment types and body parts to send, receive and retain objects in movement contexts; practise across both dominant and non-dominant body parts.
wider: Use different types of equipment to create an original movement challenge and evaluate how difficult object control was
Compare controlling objects in water versus on land, noting how the medium changes the challenge
Explore equipment from different cultural contexts, noting similarities and differences in how objects are controlled

response_modes.reason: Object control requires repetition with feedback — students benefit from focused practice on one control pattern before switching equipment or body parts.
Varying equipment types (bats, racquets, hands, feet) and object types (balls of different sizes, beanbags) broadens the range of control experiences without increasing conceptual demand.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Equipment and body-part variety produces genuinely wider experience — students who have controlled objects across multiple equipment types and both body parts have broader object-control repertoires than those who have only practised dominant-hand skills with a standard ball.
success_criteria: Uses at least one piece of equipment to send or receive a moving object
Attempts object control using a non-dominant body part in a movement activity

nodes.label: Applying skills across varied movement situations
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can practise fundamental movement skills and apply them purposefully across a variety of movement situations, including games, sequences, and object control contexts.
nodes.minimum_width: Demonstrate the same fundamental movement skill across at least two different movement situations (e.g. a game and a sequence or object control task).
nodes.typical_width: Apply a range of fundamental movement skills across varied movement situations — games, sequences, and individual and partner object control tasks — making purposeful choices about which skill to use.
wider: Design a short movement sequence that incorporates locomotor, balance and object control elements and perform it for a partner
Participate in a range of movement situations including one in an outdoor or natural setting, comparing how skills transfer
Reflect on which movement situations they find most and least enjoyable and explain how that affects how well they apply skills

response_modes.reason: This node draws together locomotor movement, skill selection, and object control into the descriptor's full demand — purposeful application across varied situations. Provide tasks that require students to draw on all three prior nodes simultaneously rather than practising each in isolation.

success_criteria: Demonstrates a fundamental movement skill in at least two different movement situations
Makes a purposeful movement choice and can describe it in at least one situation
